critique.evidence: The screen usefully reframes evaluation around PR-AUC, constrained-FPR recall, calibration, latency, fraud value caught, and good value blocked. It also shows an ablation where removing provenance lowers PR-AUC from 0.958 to 0.837. However, the evidence remains a generic fraud-model dashboard: it does not connect the metrics to Mastercard’s specific hackathon brief, transaction/payment scenarios, intent-integrity attacks, or an end-to-end defended decision. The ablations show 100% fresh-row D recall and “no change” for both removed layers, so they do not demonstrate that the intent-integrity defenses materially improve the named recall outcome. The results also lack dataset size, operating-threshold definitions, baseline comparisons, uncertainty, and traceable experiment provenance.
critique.fix: Tie every metric to a concrete Mastercard payment-intent attack and decision outcome; add defended-versus-undefended baselines at identical thresholds, dataset/sample counts and confidence bounds, and an inspectable case trace showing how semantic and provenance controls prevent harmful authorization changes. Replace or supplement the uninformative D-recall ablation with outcomes that visibly change when each defense layer is removed.
